blocks.prompt: Eyes on Top, Mouth Below
blocks.text: A stingray is built upside down for hunting. Its eyes sit on top of its head. Its mouth sits underneath, flat against the sea floor. That means a stingray never sees the crab it is about to eat. It does not need to see it. A stingray's snout is covered in tiny holes filled with jelly. Those holes can feel electricity. Every living animal makes a small amount of electricity when its muscles move. A crab hiding under the sand cannot help it. Its heart beats, its legs twitch, and the stingray feels the faint spark from above. Then the stingray settles over the spot and pumps water out of its mouth to blow the sand away. Underneath is the crab. The stingray's teeth are not sharp points. They are flat plates, made for crushing shells. The tail is a different story. The barb near the base of the tail is only for defense. A stingray never hunts with it. It stings when something big steps on it, and then it swims away.

blocks.prompt: The Shark That Lay Down
blocks.text: Pick up a stingray's skeleton and you will not find a single bone. Like sharks, rays are built from cartilage, the same bendy stuff inside your ears and the tip of your nose. Rays and sharks are close relatives. The simplest way to picture a ray is to imagine a shark that lay down flat on the sea floor and stayed there. Lying flat solves one problem and creates several. It makes a ray almost invisible from above, especially once it flicks sand over its back. But a fish that rests on the bottom has a problem with breathing. Most fish pull water in through the mouth and push it out over the gills. A ray's mouth is pressed against the sand, so it would swallow grit with every breath. The answer sits just behind its eyes: two holes called spiracles. The ray draws in clean water from above through the spiracles and sends it down over the gills on its underside. Being flat causes a second problem. With eyes on top and a mouth beneath, a ray cannot look at its food. Instead it reads the water. Its snout is dotted with jelly-filled pores that detect faint electric fields. A clam buried in the sand gives itself away every time its muscles move. The ray hovers, feels the signal, blows the sand off with a jet of water, and crushes the shell with teeth shaped like flat plates. The famous barb is not a hunting tool. It is a serrated spine near the base of the tail, and a ray uses it only when something heavy pins it down. If it breaks off, a new one grows.

blocks.prompt: The Sixth Sense in the Sand
blocks.text: Every animal leaks electricity. A muscle cannot contract without generating a tiny electrical field, and a heart cannot beat without broadcasting one. On land, that signal disappears almost instantly, because air is a poor conductor. Salt water is an excellent one. In the ocean, a hidden animal is quietly announcing itself, and the stingray has spent more than a hundred million years learning to listen. The listening organs are called ampullae of Lorenzini. They are pores scattered across the ray's snout and underside, each one opening into a canal filled with clear jelly and ending at a bundle of sensory cells. The jelly carries an electric field down to those cells with almost no loss. The system is astonishingly sensitive. Rays and their shark relatives can detect fields measured in billionths of a volt, which is roughly like noticing a flashlight battery switched on across a stretch of ocean. This sense solves a design problem. A stingray's eyes sit on top of its head and its mouth sits underneath, so it is structurally incapable of watching its own meal. It does not have to. It cruises a few inches above the sand, reading the electrical noise below it. A clam that has buried itself perfectly, motionless and invisible, is still pumping water through its body, and every pump is a small announcement. The ray stops, settles, and fires a jet of water from its mouth to strip the sand away. Its teeth are fused into flat crushing plates that break the shell like a nutcracker. The tail barb is often the only thing people know about stingrays, and it is the least interesting part. It is a defensive spine, serrated and coated in venomous tissue, and a ray deploys it only when it is trapped or stepped on. The venom is made of proteins, which fall apart in heat, which is why the standard first aid is to soak the wound in water as hot as the person can stand. Rays are not aggressive. Wade into shallow water in ray country and the advice is simply to shuffle your feet. A stingray that feels you coming will leave long before you arrive.

Skeleton is cartilage, no bone at all
Pectoral fins fused to the head form the disc
Spiracles on top draw in clean water
Ampullae of Lorenzini sense billionths of a volt

blocks.prompt: The Shark That Lay Down: A Study in Trade-Offs
blocks.text: Evolution does not design. It edits, and every edit costs something. The stingray is one of the clearest illustrations of that principle in the ocean, because almost every strange thing about a ray is the bill for a single decision made a very long time ago: lie down. Rays are cartilaginous fish. Their skeletons contain no bone at all, only cartilage, the same flexible tissue in the tip of your nose. That places them in the same group as sharks, and the family resemblance is closer than it looks. A useful, if crude, way to picture a ray is a shark that pressed itself flat against the sea floor and never got up. Its body was compressed from top to bottom, its pectoral fins spread outward and fused to its head until they became a disc, and it began to move by rippling the edges of that disc rather than sweeping a tail. Watch a stingray cross open water and the word that comes to mind is not swimming. It is flying. The advantages were immediate. A flat animal lying on sand casts almost no shadow and breaks no outline, and a few flicks of the wings bury it entirely. But flattening broke things too, and each break required a repair. Consider breathing. A typical fish draws water in through its mouth and passes it over the gills. A ray's mouth is on its underside, pressed into sediment, so drawing water in that way would mean inhaling sand. The repair is a pair of openings called spiracles, set behind the eyes on the animal's upper surface. Water enters there, clean, and exits over the gill slits below. Consider hunting. Eyes migrated to the top of the disc while the mouth stayed on the bottom. A ray is therefore incapable, as a matter of anatomy, of seeing what it is about to eat. The repair was already in the family. Sharks and rays share an electrical sense, housed in pores called ampullae of Lorenzini, each a jelly-filled canal that carries faint electric fields to sensory cells. Muscle movement generates such fields, salt water conducts them beautifully, and a clam buried out of sight is still pumping. The ray hovers, reads the sand, jets water from its mouth to excavate, and crushes the shell with teeth fused into flat plates. Consider defense. Flat, slow, and pinned to the bottom is an excellent way to be eaten by a shark. The repair is the barb: a serrated spine near the base of the tail, sheathed in venomous tissue, that a cornered ray drives upward. It is worth being precise here. The barb is never used for hunting. It is used when something large is already on top of the animal. It can also break off and grow back. Even reproduction follows the same cautious logic. Rays do not scatter eggs and hope. The young develop inside the mother, first on yolk and then on a nutritious fluid the uterine lining secretes, and they are born as small, complete, working rays. Which leaves the reputation. Most people know exactly one fact about stingrays, and it is the one fact that describes the animal least. A ray's entire body is an argument for avoidance: hide, feel, feed, leave. The spine is the last line of a defense that would rather not be reached at all, which is why the standard advice in shallow water is not to watch for rays but to shuffle your feet. Give the animal a warning and it will do what its whole body is built to do. It will go.
